title: Water supply and hydrosocial scarcity in the Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Area
overall_rob_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (3 Can't tell and 2 No items across Q1-Q9)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically documents municipal drinking-water network connection deficits and severe supply intermittency in peripheral municipalities of the Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Area using IBGE census data, municipal sanitation diagnostics, and interviews with utility staff, its explanatory focus is macro-level infrastructure planning, incomplete physical supply networks (insufficient treatment capacity, conduits, and distribution reservoirs), capital investment ineffectiveness by CEDAE, and bulk-water river-basin drought/reservoir management rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included.

title: Water, rural population and administration techniques: the case of Jequitinhonha Valley, Minas Gerais
overall_rob_rating: Moderate concern (3 Can't tell, 1 No items)
rationale: Excluded at full text as E01 (Wrong topic — natural water-resources management and cultural ecology rather than household/community water or sanitation service access; also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification). Based on qualitative interviews with 188 rural farming families in 22 communities of the Jequitinhonha Valley (1999–2002), Ribeiro & Galizoni (2003) examine peasant cultural perceptions of natural water ('água fina' from flowing springs vs. 'água grande' in rivers; water as a divine gift 'dom') and informal customary sharing of springs across agricultural micro-watersheds, contrasting these 'direct consumers' ('consumidores diretos') of natural water sources with bulk water-resources governance under Brazil's Law No. 9.433/1997 (ANA, river basin committees, bulk 'outorga' and pricing for hydropower/irrigation). It does not study water or sanitation service access (mentioning drought tanker trucks, rainwater cisterns, and post-migration village municipal supply only peripherally), and Law 9.433/1997 had not even been implemented locally in the studied basins (PDF pp. 6, 14), so no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation service access is empirically examined.

title: Infrastructure in informal settlements: co-production of public services for inclusive governance
overall_rob_rating: Moderate concern (3 Can't tell / 2 No items)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. This ethnographic case study investigates how donor- and NGO-supported communal sanitation 'bio-centres' introduced under Nairobi's participatory slum-upgrading programme (KENSUP) become locally embedded through everyday 'place-making' (leading either to CBO spin-off projects or to youth livelihood appropriation and drug dealing) and argues for ongoing post-construction monitoring and deliberative co-production among CBOs, NGOs, and City Council planners. While the paper passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include') as an empirical study of participatory urban sanitation governance and co-production, and while one interview passage in Section 5.3 notes in passing that a spun-off CBO needed the Chief's written permission and bureaucratic permits to connect its water pipe to Nairobi City Water Services and install a water tank, the paper does not examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing service access as its exposure; instead, its focus is participatory project delivery, socio-spatial embeddedness, and collaborative project follow-up. Confidence is rated medium because of the brief descriptive evidence on permitting hurdles delaying municipal water-pipe connection in one sub-case.

title: Urban Sprawl and Drinking Water Services in an African City: The Case of Bukavu in DR Congo
overall_rob_rating: High methodological concern / Low overall quality (per MMAT 2018 guidance, no numeric score is computed and overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component: major methodological and reporting limitations affect both the qualitative interview/archival component and the quantitative cross-sectional household/GIS component)
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the active 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although the study empirically examines household drinking water access in Bukavu (n = 655 households plus GIS analysis) and discusses broad urban governance challenges, historical urban master plans, and neighborhood land tenure informality (which would satisfy the plain literal wording of Criterion 2), its actual exposure is physical and demographic urban sprawl, distance from the city center, geomorphological hazards, and REGIDESO production/maintenance deficits. It does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household water service access (such as tenure/documentation eligibility requirements for utility connection, administrative burdens in water applications, tariff/cost-recovery rules, or regulatory structure).

title: Integration and implementation of rainwater harvesting technologies in development programs, planning and budgeting in Matungulu Sub-County, Machakos County, Kenya
chosen_rob_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
rationale: Excluded primarily for wrong exposure (E03) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type scope of Criterion 2, and secondarily for lacking an eligible water service-access outcome (Criterion 4). Although the paper passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 by examining county government planning, budgeting, and programmatic support for rainwater harvesting technologies (RHTs), its empirical exposure consists solely of generic project delivery and promotional/capacity-building activities (farmer training, awareness creation, excavation of water pans/dams, group funding, and tank provision), with Kenya's 2010 Constitution and Water Act 2016 discussed only as unanalysed background and no rule-type mechanism governing service access examined. Furthermore, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = 'exclude'), the paper would still be excluded because its tested empirical outcome is an undefined composite 'Impact on Household Livelihoods' score rather than a water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome (and its focus is farm-household RHT adoption rather than water service access). Statistical significance of the reported regression (p < 0.05) played zero role in this decision.

title: Costs and willingness to pay for pit latrine emptying services in Kigali, Rwanda
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Although the paper empirically examines household sanitation service uptake and affordability (pit latrine emptying in informal settlements of Kigali, Rwanda), its empirical exposures are market willingness-to-pay attributes, promotional coupon price levels and group-empty discounts offered by an unregulated private social enterprise (Pit Vidura), and operational truck-scale cost scenarios rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, or public-utility tariff/governance rule directly governing service access. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it examines consumer valuation of formalized/registered enterprise delivery versus informal day laborers, volumetric versus flat-fee pricing formats, and a covariate for household versus landlord financial responsibility for pit maintenance; however, none of these constitutes an analyzed rule-type legal or administrative mechanism under the active 2026-10-13 scope clarification (and municipal cross-subsidy surcharges or forthcoming sealing bans are discussed only hypothetically or as unmeasured context).

title: Exclusionary Policies in Urban Development, How under-servicing of migrant households affects the growth and composition of Brazilian cities
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification of Criterion 2 (whereas under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 it would be included). Although the paper empirically models household central water connection rates for small (1-3 room) urban houses in Brazil (Section 4), what the authors term 'exclusionary policy' is municipal infrastructure under-provision itself, explicitly defined regardless of formal land title or compliance with land-use regulations. The empirical determinants of water connection coverage tested in Section 4 are inter-municipal Tiebout/Brueckner strategic competition (other localities' water coverage), locality median income, locality size, their interaction, population density, and 1982 anti-military vote shares — not a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, rule-application discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Pre-1988 legal restrictions on servicing informal settlements vs. post-1988 democratization serve only as unanalysed macro-governance background, local minimum lot-size zoning laws (Section 2.5) are not linked to water/sanitation access, and Section 5 treats water connection coverage as the exposure predicting city population growth rather than as the outcome.

title: Assessing the sustainability of urban water supply systems in Shillong, India
rationale: reason: "full text not accessible" — The retrieved cached PDF matches the record metadata (Kharmylliem & Kipgen 2021, DOI 10.1163/15691497-12341594), but contains only a 2-page Brill publisher preview (pp. 251–252 of pp. 251–277) comprising the title, abstract, keywords, and the first five paragraphs of the introduction, cutting off mid-sentence at the bottom of p. 252. title: Piped water revenue and investment strategies in rural Africa
rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). Although this longitudinal empirical study of rural piped water operators in Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda examines rule-type tariff levels, cost-recovery/payment collection modalities (prepaid credit meters vs pay-as-you-fetch and monthly billing), and public vs enterprise ownership/contracting models (satisfying Criterion 2 under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), its empirical outcome in all statistical tests and GEE models is operator financial revenue ($/m3 and $/service area/month). The authors explicitly state that missing user population counts prevent measuring service area penetration or per-capita water consumption, that consecutive zero-revenue months were dropped regardless of water usage because nonpayment is not studied, and that reliability and actual user prices paid (affordability) are unobserved. Confidence is set to medium because Tables 3 and 4 report descriptive summary statistics on aggregate volume dispensed per waterpoint (m3/waterpoint/month), though this reflects waterpoint dispensing capacity/throughput (mixing community kiosks, household taps, and institutional taps without user denominators) rather than an analysed user access or consumption-quantity outcome.

title: Financing Municipal Water and Sanitation Services in Nairobi’s Informal Settlements
retrieval_source: gdrive:1B_POjhFhNHoNusL08osgbLFa43scoopY (R4D81D56EA98B__Financing Municipal Water and Sanitation Serv)
rationale: This NBER working paper meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It reports two randomized field experiments in Nairobi's informal settlements, one of which directly evaluates systematic contract enforcement of utility service disconnection rules for arrears on water/sewer bills and subsidized connection loans—incorporating explicit arrears thresholds, formal notices, financial hardship exemptions/payment plans, physical disconnections, and flexible reconnection discretion—and measures nine-month impacts on compound piped water and sanitation connections, working connection status, primary water source, metered consumption, water expenditure, and fetching time (with quantitative estimates extractable for synthesis). Null treatment effects on endline water and sanitation access do not affect eligibility.

title: Countdown 2015: an assessment of basic provision to migrant families in the urban slums of Ludhiana, North India
retrieval_source: gdrive:1QwDTXEpO00XcYfVEdg1finmTn-5JBsUU (Sengupta and Benjamin - 2016 - Countdown 2015 an assessment )
chosen_rob_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
rationale: This cross-sectional empirical survey of 3,947 migrant households in Ludhiana, India directly compares household drinking-water supply, toilet access/open defecation, and drainage across statutory slum notification categories (15 notified slums vs. 15 non-notified slums and open spaces). Because formal notification under a Slum Act is a rule-type legal/administrative classification that obliges municipal authorities to provide water and sanitation services and governs settlement eligibility for municipal infrastructure, the study satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2.

title: Spectacular infrastructure and its breakdown in socialist Vietnam
overall_rob_rating: Moderate methodological concern (3 Can't tell items: Q4, Q7, Q8; 0 No items)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although this ethnographic and archival study examines household water and sanitation conditions in a Vietnamese social housing complex (c1=yes, c3=yes, c4=yes) and discusses socialist urban governance, state housing allocation, and post-Doi moi apartment privatization in broad terms (so plain_criterion2_decision is "include"), it does not analyze a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access. Water deprivation on upper floors in the postwar era resulted from engineering/hydraulic pressure limitations and municipal fiscal shortages following East German reconstruction project delivery, while contemporary disputes center on physical building decay, indoor leaks after regular water access was restored in the mid-1990s, and moral expectations of state paternalism rather than rules governing water/sanitation access.

title: Strategies for Achieving Sustainability of Water Supply Systems in Rural Environments with Community Management in Brazil
overall_rob_rating: Weak-to-adequate institutional evidence (structured non-validated judgment; adequate multiscale institutional mapping but weak empirical validation due to convenience sampling of N=11 experts, unvalidated binary opinion polling, and absence of empirical outcome measurement)
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2 and Criterion 5). This paper formulates a normative multiscale action plan for community-managed rural water supply systems in Brazil based on a narrative literature review and secondary background on Ceará's SISAR model, and validates the proposed strategies through binary ('yes'/'no') face-to-face interviews with 11 rural water and sanitation specialists (Tables 2–4). The only primary outcome reported is the count of experts voting 'In Favor' vs. 'Against' each proposed strategy; no empirical outcome measuring household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is reported. Moreover, under the 2026-10-13 narrow Criterion 2 reading, no operational rule-type mechanism governing service access is empirically examined (only broad normative policy, engineering, support, and tariff/regulatory recommendations are proposed). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because it lacks any empirical water-access outcome.
